content: Post-graduate year (PGY) is a term used in North America to describe the progression of medical residents in their training programs after graduating from medical school. This numerical system is employed to stratify levels of responsibility within residency programs and to determine salary scales for residents. The duration of a residency program is largely dependent on the medical specialty chosen by the graduate. For instance, specialties such as family medicine and internal medicine typically require three years of residency training. In contrast, surgical specialties generally necessitate a minimum of five years of training. Further subspecialization, such as vascular surgery or orthopedic spine surgery, extends the duration of post-graduate training beyond the standard residency period. For detailed information about specific medical residency programs, one can refer to the American Medical Association's Fellowship and Residency Electronic Interactive Database. Pharmacy residencies, which are gaining popularity, also adopt the PGY nomenclature. In this context, PGY-1 refers to the general pharmacy practice residency, which serves as the foundational training year. PGY-2, often optional, allows for specialization in areas such as critical care, cardiology, oncology, and other advanced pharmacy fields.
